phonemes.desc: Open-mid back rounded vowel [ɔ] with low tone; the initial vowel is written without dot below in the lexical form.
Voiced alveolar lateral approximant [l] followed by close-mid back rounded vowel [o] with high tone.
Voiced alveolar stop [d] followed by close back rounded vowel [u] with low tone.
Voiced bilabial nasal [m] followed by open [a] with high tone.
Voiced alveolar tap or trill [r] followed by mid front vowel [e] with low tone.

pronunciation.approximation: aw-loh-doo-MAH-reh — low 'aw', high 'loh', low 'doo', high 'MAH', low 'reh'.

kin.label: Yoruba
kin.form: Olódùmarè, the Supreme Creator and owner of the universe — the name is traditionally glossed as 'owner of the source of fullness' (orí-ọ̀dú, 'source-head', plus máre, 'that which is full').

kin.label: Lucumí
kin.form: Olodumare, the remote high god who delegates the orishas.

kin.label: Related title
kin.form: Olódùmarè is sometimes addressed as Olorun ('Owner of Heaven').

pronunciation.note: Olódùmarè is Tier 1: the acute accent on ó preserves a high tone and the grave accents on ù and è preserve low tones, distinctive features the ASCII form loses. Tonal distinctions are crucial to Yoruba meaning.

domains.title: Owner of the Universe
domains.subtitle: Supreme Creator, Destiny, and Final Authority
domains.lead: Olódùmarè is the high god of Yoruba religion — the sole creator and owner of heaven, earth, and every breath that moves within them. Remote and self-sufficient, he receives no images and depends on no offerings; the orishas govern the world, but only as his delegates. He assigns destiny and stands beyond all appeal.

cards.name: Supreme Creator
cards.desc: He alone creates ex nihilo; the orishas shape and govern what he has made.

cards.name: Destiny
cards.desc: He assigns àkúnlẹ̀yàn, the destiny chosen by each soul before birth, and ratifies it with the breath of life.

cards.name: Final Authority
cards.desc: No orisha can override his decree; even Ọrúnmìlà interprets rather than changes fate.

cards.name: Transcendence
cards.desc: He needs no temple image; he is worshipped through the sky, the sun, and the breath of life.

symbols.name: The sky (ọ̀run)
symbols.meaning: His visible throne; the firmament is his temple and his garment.

symbols.name: The rainbow-serpent (ọ̀ṣùmàrè)
symbols.meaning: The celestial serpent-arch whose appearance seals the passage between heaven and earth; revered as an orisha in its own right and a sign of Olódùmarè's covenant with the sky.

symbols.name: Cool wind and breath (éémí)
symbols.meaning: The invisible life-force he breathes into the bodies shaped by Ọbatalá; the felt proof of the remote god in every living chest.

symbols.name: White light
symbols.meaning: Pure, imageless presence; Olódùmarè has no anthropomorphic cult statue anywhere in Yorubaland.

mythology.lead: Olódùmarè's mythology is theology: the origin of the world, the distribution of destiny, and the hierarchy between the high god and the orishas who serve him.

myths.title: The Chain from Heaven
myths.text: At the beginning the world was water below and sky above, and Olódùmarè resolved to make a place for life. He charged Ọbatalá (Orishanla) with the task: descend the golden chain from heaven carrying a snail shell filled with sand, a five-toed hen, and a chameleon to test the ground. But at the threshold the trickster Ẹṣù offered Ọbatalá palm wine; he drank, grew drowsy, and slept. His younger brother Odùduwà seized the chain, the shell, and the hen, scattered the sand on the primordial flood, and the hen scratched it into the ridges of the earth (Ifá corpus; retold by E. Bolaji Idowu, Olódùmarè: God in Yoruba Belief, 1962). When Ọbatalá awoke and descended, the work was done; humbled, he accepted as his own share the moulding of human bodies from clay. The myth divides creation into command, execution, and embodiment: Olódùmarè wills the world, others build it, and the god whom failure humbled receives the clay of humanity.

myths.title: The Potter Àjàlá and the Unborn Heads
myths.text: Before birth, every soul kneels in heaven to choose a destiny — àkúnlẹ̀yàn, 'that which is chosen kneeling' — from the moulds of Àjàlá, the divine potter of heads (orí). Ifá verses do not flatter the potter: Àjàlá is a drunkard whose wares are badly fired, and some heads are cracked, some crooked, while only the patient find the sound ones. The choice made, Olódùmarè himself ratifies it and breathes the éémí, the life-force, into the chosen head — and because the seal is his, destiny can be softened by sacrifice and wisdom but never revoked (Idowu 1962; Abimbola, Ifá: An Exposition of Ifá Literary Corpus, 1976). Idowu reads the myth as Yoruba theodicy in miniature: the world is not unjust because Olódùmarè is cruel, but because choosing is the price of being human — and heaven itself keeps a careless potter.

myths.title: The Flood and the Forgetful People
myths.text: Early accounts of Yoruba cosmogony record a flood sent by Olódùmarè when humanity grew numerous, neglected sacrifice, and forgot the source of its breath (J. Olumide Lucas, The Religion of the Yorubas, 1948; Idowu 1962). The waters rose until only a remnant remained; in the most told form a man, a woman, and a faithful dog endured, and from them the earth was repeopled. The tale belongs to the universal flood type, yet it answers a specifically Yoruba question: why does the most generous god become the most terrible? Because sustenance is a loan, not a possession — when gratitude fails entirely, the owner reclaims the universe he lent. The flood myth also explains Olódùmarè's remoteness as a mercy: a god this absolute cannot be approached directly, and the orishas exist precisely to stand between his justice and human fragility.

myths.title: Why the Owner of the Universe Needs No Temple
myths.text: Yoruba theologians explain the high god's cultlessness by turning it into doctrine: no carver can depict him, no drumbeat can summon him, and no sacrifice can add anything to him (Idowu 1962). Prayer reaches him through the sky itself; his witnesses are the sun and the rainbow-serpent, and his éémí already fills every living body. Idowu notes that the absence of a priesthood is the theology — Olódùmarè is complete in himself, and a god who needs nothing from mortals cannot be bargained with. Yet this absence structures the entire religion: because the owner of the universe will not come down, the orishas must. Every orisha festival thus honours him secondhand, and every breath of éémí is a liturgy no priest need perform. The mythology of his remoteness is thus the charter of Yoruba polytheism itself — one absolute source, and a world governed by delegates.

lore.syncretism: Because Olódùmarè is a remote, imageless high god, he was readily mapped onto the Christian God by enslaved Yoruba people and their descendants. In Cuban Santería and Brazilian Candomblé, Olódumare is identified with the transcendent Creator, while the orishas correspond to saints and angels. In the scholarship this is called parallelismo rather than simple substitution: each orisha kept its own name, colours, and drum while accepting a Catholic 'cover'. The theological structure — one high god above a host of intermediaries — let the Yoruba pantheon survive inside monotheistic frameworks without losing its polytheistic texture, and in recent decades the diaspora has exported the model back to Nigeria itself.
lore.culturalLegacy: Olódùmarè remains the theological centre of Yoruba religion and its diaspora. The idiom 'Olódùmarè willing' structures daily speech, and the doctrine that destiny is chosen but ratified by the high god shapes Yoruba ethics of responsibility and sacrifice. In African philosophy he is a key figure in debates over monotheism and polytheism, destiny and freedom — Idowu's classic study made him a proof that African theology possesses a doctrine of God as rigorous as any. His name echoes through reggae, Afrobeat, and global spirituality as a byword for the supreme source, a standing reminder that African theology has always made room for the One beyond the many.
lore.extendedMeditation:
Olódùmarè is the god who needs nothing. He does not eat sacrifices the way the orishas do; he does not possess dancers or demand festivals. He simply is — the owner of the universe, the breath in every body, the sky above every shrine. This makes him easy to overlook and impossible to escape.

In a religious landscape full of colourful, approachable deities, Olódùmarè is the silence behind the drum. He asks us to distinguish between what we need and what we want, between the god who answers prayers and the source from which prayer itself arises. To remember him is to remember that the orishas, however powerful, are not ultimate. Something older owns even them — and breathes, at this moment, in you.

lore.archaeology: As a transcendent deity without anthropomorphic cult images, Olódùmarè leaves few direct archaeological traces, and that absence is itself the primary evidence of the theology. Sky-oriented prayer sites across Yorubaland — open-air enclosures without idols, oriented to the sunrise — match Idowu's description of a god worshipped through light and breath. His presence is inferred from the cosmological vocabulary of Ifá verses recorded by Bascom and Abimbola and from the white-cloth, empty-throne symbolism placed above orisha altars in Cuban Santería and Brazilian Candomblé houses, where the transcendent Creator is represented precisely by what is absent: an unoccupied seat under the sky.
